_comment: OVERLAY on seed-profile-i8.json, which is itself an overlay on the measured
seed-profile.json. Campaign S1 — the vacuity fix.
WHY THIS EXISTS. S1's first full run produced a disposition table with zero blanks and
three surfaces that meant nothing: get_recent_events, get_top_events and get_top_outbound
returned EMPTY on BOTH arms. Empty compares equal to empty, so those three reported
agreement while proving that neither arm had been asked a question the corpus could
answer. That is PITFALLS 44's shape exactly, and PITFALLS 38's before it.
A fourth surface failed from the other side. EXPECTED-DIFFS R16 predicts that
get_max_and_average_pages_per_visit rises when count(ip) becomes count(*) — which can only
happen if some row HAS a NULL ip. The seeder had never written one, so the two arms agreed
for a reason that has nothing to do with the fix, and R16 was unfalsifiable rather than
confirmed. A prediction that cannot fail is not evidence.
EVERY KNOB HERE IS OFF IN THE BASE PROFILES. A caller that does not pass this overlay seeds
the corpus it always seeded, byte for byte, because each new column is written as NULL at
rate 0 — the same value the table held when the column was absent from the INSERT. Runs
already recorded against the I8 fixture stay valid.
THE RATES ARE CHOSEN TO DISCRIMINATE, NOT TO BE REALISTIC. This is the question PITFALLS 22
demands of any fixture: what number does the check produce WITH the defect and WITHOUT it?
Each rate below is set where those two numbers differ by more than sampling noise on a
150k-row corpus, and the reason is stated per knob.

_why_ip: R16's discriminator. count(ip) skips NULLs and count(*) does not, so the two forms differ
by exactly the NULL count. At 0 they are identical and R16 cannot fail; at 0.04 a 150k-row
corpus carries ~6,000 rows the old form drops — a difference no rounding can hide, while
staying far below a rate that would distort the pageviews-per-visit mean the same report
Production really does have NULL ips (a tracked hit whose address was unresolvable), so
this makes the fixture MORE like production, not less.

_why_events: 0.30 attaches an event to roughly three pageviews in ten. Half are custom `event:` rows
and half are `type:click` rows, because BOTH event reports exclude notes LIKE
'type:click%' — seeding only clicks leaves them empty, which is how the first version of
this overlay failed to fix the vacuity it was written for.
get_top_events groups by NOTES (not by event_description, which it never selects), over 12
distinct custom notes. Twelve is what makes the report's row limit bind on a corpus where
the limit is the default 20 only after other filters — and more to the point, twelve groups
each holding hundreds of rows means a dropped GROUP BY or a date filter that stopped
applying MOVES a number instead of leaving zero. An earlier draft claimed twelve while the
seeder delivered six, because the note kind and the description index were both keyed on
the row id: the seeder now indexes on (id DIV 2) so the two are independent.
Also feeds Pro's heat map, which filters position LIKE '%,%': the seeded rows carry real
coordinates so that surface is exercisable rather than vacuous one layer out.
_why_outbound: 0.08 of pageviews carry an outbound link across 60 distinct targets. get_top_outbound is
a LIMIT 20 report, so 60 targets means the cut line falls INSIDE the data — a report that
returned everything, or truncated at the wrong place, differs from one that does not. At
fewer than 20 distinct targets the limit would never bind and the surface would be green
no matter what the code did to it.
_why_searchterms: 0.12 of ENTRY pageviews arrive with a search query. Only entry rows carry them, matching
how the tracker records a landing — seeding them on internal navigation would make the
search report count one arrival many times, which is the defect shape M2 records for
_why_loggedin: 0.02 of pageviews are logged-in hits carrying both a `loggedin:` note and the username to
group by. Pro's last-login report greps notes LIKE '%loggedin:%' and groups by username
over 40 users; 2% of 150k is ~3,000 rows, so MAX(dt) per user has real spread instead of
resolving from one row each. Run 46 measured that query on the live 443k table and chose
